description: Cipher-X Crew is a virtual team under Universal Event exploring the mystery of Planet X using NASA's SPHEREx data. We aim to detect subtle shifts, map cosmic patterns, and build a visual tool for redshift anomalies. Passionate about space, AI, and storytelling. We are two members from Pakistan, looking for creative minds to join our cosmic hunt! Let's decode the universe together.
summary: NASA's SPHEREx telescope is photographing the whole sky in infrared, again and again — but almost nobody ever watches those images change. Watch the Sky Change turns real SPHEREx archive observations into a living observatory: choose one of the challenge's five benchmark targets — Barnard's Star, Epsilon Indi, WISE 0855, RW Aurigae or R Draconis — or the interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS, and play back its genuine archive frames to see the sky move. A difference view erases every fixed star so only what moved or changed remains, and a field-of-view selector lets visitors zoom into the field. This is not a simulation: every frame is a real SPHEREx level-2 observation with its true UTC time, detector and wavelength band. We even measured the comet's motion from our own frames — 1.154° per day, within about 1% of the JPL-validated rate. Tools like this are how slow, faint movers — the Planet X regime — will be found: not in single images, but in change itself.
details:
Live demo: https://sanaasif1217.github.io/cipher-x-crew/
Source code: https://github.com/sanaasif1217/cipher-x-crew

WHAT IT DOES

Watch the Sky Change is a public observatory built on NASA's SPHEREx survey.

SPHEREx is photographing the entire sky in infrared, over and over — but those images are usually buried in archives that only specialists can use. Our project brings them to everyone.

In the "Real Data" section, visitors choose one of six targets — the five benchmark targets named in the challenge brief (Barnard's Star, Epsilon Indi, WISE 0855, RW Aurigae and R Draconis) plus the interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS — and play back twelve genuine SPHEREx observations of that field, watching the sky actually change over time.

Every frame carries its real UTC time, detector and wavelength band.

Around the frames sits a working observatory:
• a field-of-view selector (0.50 / 0.30 / 0.18 degrees)
• an Epoch Explorer listing every observation's metadata
• brightness analytics measured live in the browser
• a Compare mode for viewing two targets side by side
• a guided tour for first-time visitors
• a Research Assistant that answers questions from the project's own documents and cites its sources

HOW IT WORKS

A Python backend (FastAPI, Astropy) builds the data packs:

It queries the IRSA TAP service for SPHEREx level-2 observations of each target — between 129 and 1,258 observations per field

It downloads cutouts and reprojects them onto a common grid with one global stretch

It renders a data pack: twelve frames plus a manifest recording each frame's UTC, observation ID, collection, detector and band

The packs live in our public GitHub repository, and the website (React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS) loads them directly — so the live observatory runs with no server at all.

The centrepiece is the Difference view: subtracting the first frame from every later frame makes all fixed stars vanish, so only what moved or changed brightness remains — the exact technique astronomers use to hunt moving objects.

A MEASURED RESULT

This project does not just display data — it measures it.

The comet pack spans 04:26 to 19:09 UTC on 14 December 2025. We centroided the comet's light in 9 of its 12 frames (in the last three it has left the field) and fitted its motion:

• 173 arcsec per hour
• 1.154 degrees per day, at position angle 289.1 degrees
• A journey of 1,426 arcsec across 8.2 hours

An independent fit to the underlying SPHEREx epochs, validated against NASA JPL's Horizons ephemeris, gives 1.167 degrees per day at 289.3 degrees.

Our measurement agrees within about 1 percent.

The measurement script and its results file are in the repository, so any judge can reproduce our number.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

SPHEREx will image the whole sky repeatedly for years — and the discoveries in that flood of data live in the differences between epochs:

• asteroids
• comets
• variable stars
• and possibly slow, distant worlds

Yet the archive is unusable for anyone without specialist tools.

Our intended impact is to close that gap: a free, honest, working tool that lets students, teachers and citizen scientists:

• see real survey data change
• understand how moving objects are found
• and even check a measured result for themselves

If tools like this succeed, the search for faint, slow movers — the Planet X regime — gains thousands of extra eyes.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

First, the product is change itself: instead of a gallery of static images, the sky is a film you can play, rewind and interrogate.

Second, the Difference view turns a professional detection technique into a single click that anyone can understand in seconds — fixed stars disappear, motion remains.

Third, the project closes the loop from display to science: the same frames a visitor watches were used to produce a validated measurement.

Fourth, honesty is designed in, not added on: presentation visuals and real archive data are kept in separate, clearly labelled sections, so nothing simulated is ever presented as data. Even our Research Assistant follows the same principle — it answers only from our documents, cites its source, and openly says when it does not know.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGY

Data: NASA SPHEREx level-2 observations via the IRSA archive (IPAC/Caltech), IRSA TAP queries and image cutout services; NASA JPL Horizons ephemeris as the independent validation reference.

Backend: Python with Astropy, NumPy, SciPy and Pillow; FastAPI.

Frontend: React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, GSAP. Hosting and version control: GitHub and GitHub Pages, under an MIT licence.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

We optimised for trust.

(1) Authenticity: real archive data only, with full provenance on every frame.

(2) Honesty: clear separation and labelling of visualisation versus data, limitations stated openly, and AI assistance disclosed in our README and in this submission, as the rules require.

(3) Accessibility: no installs, no server, works in any modern browser, with a guided tour so a first-time visitor understands the project in a minute.

(4) Reproducibility: the pipeline, the measurement script and all results are public in the repository.

LIMITATIONS AND FUTURE WORK

Each pack samples twelve frames from a much deeper archive; brightness analytics use the rendered frames rather than calibrated fluxes; and the comet measurement centroids around an ephemeris prediction rather than performing blind detection. The backend can already generate a data pack for arbitrary coordinates through its API — hosting it so visitors can request new patches live is our main next step, along with calibrated per-detector coadds.

TEAM

  2. Sujal Khanolkar — Team Member (website design and frontend).
